newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish bonds positive on EU pact, spread steady.
newsitem.headline: Spanish bonds positive on EU pact, spread steady.

text.p: Spain's bonos were firm on Monday mirroring a higher probability European Monetary Union would start on time after a stability pact reached at a Dublin summit.
But dealers said the differential with long Bund yields could not dip much further than the recent low level.

Earlier on the cash market, 10-year bond yields hit a record low against their German counterparts at 104 basis points, supported by the euphoria over the EU deal. But dealers said the 100 level would be difficult to break for three to six months.
"The pact breathed a lot of life into the markets. The trend is mildly positive," said Roberto Knop, analyst at Analistas Financieros Internationales (AFI).

The agreement European leaders reached last Friday in Dublin on a mechanism ensuring fiscal discipline after the launch of the single currency was welcomed by markets, especially by the peripheral ones, like Spain's.
It increased the probability they would soon be part of the Euro market, dealers said.
"Spain's market will soon stop being a peripheral one and it will become a core one," Emilio Sainz at Natwest in Madrid said.
For the Spanish market, an increased probability that the EMU will start on time is important.

"For markets this pact is important because it shows a higher commitment toward EMU, and this is making it a big deal, especially from the point of view of the peripheral markets," said Henrik Lumholdt, economist at Bank of America.
But bonos have already risen a lot in anticipation of Spain being a part of the EMU's core countries in 1999.

JP Morgan's EMU calculator, which measures the probability of a country entering EMU by market prices, is putting Spain at 80 percent probability, 10 basis points more than five days ago and 27 basis points more than 20 days ago.
Dealers and analysts said bonos were already pricing in the higher probability to enter EMU.
The 10-year spread over Bunds, which was trading at 107 bps at 1120 GMT, fell from more than 500 bps over the summer and from 330 in March.
"The year could end with a spread around 100 bps, but it will be difficult to break this level without more positive fundamentals," said Knop.
After a lower-than-expected November CPI with a year-on-year rise at 3.2 percent from 3.5 percent in October, analysts are now expecting it to break below three percent in January 1997.
At the same time the peseta strengthened against the mark, with the German currency having weakened generally in Europe after news of the stability pact.
But fears of Bank of Spain intervention to keep the currency above the 84.10 level were holding the currency back, dealers said.
"The peseta has extended its advance from Friday's announcement of the EU pact, but there's a certain fear of Bank of Spain intervention at levels between 84.05-84.10 to the mark," one trader said.
And a seasonal lack of liquidity was also playing its part in restraining the Spanish currency, dealers said.
-- Madrid Newsroom, + 341 585 8340
